# The Kalman Filter {#sec-kf}

In 1960 Rudolf Kalman published a recursive solution to the linear filtering
problem [@kalman1960]. Within a few years Stanley Schmidt's group at NASA Ames
had adapted it for Apollo midcourse navigation, and it has been the default
answer to "how do I blend a motion model with noisy sensors?" ever since. Your
phone runs several of them. So does nearly every aircraft, ship, and spacecraft
that knows where it is.

@sec-bayes gave the exact recursion for any belief. This chapter makes that
recursion cheap by making two assumptions: the models are linear, and every
noise source is Gaussian. Under those assumptions a Gaussian belief stays
Gaussian forever, so the filter only has to carry a mean vector and a covariance
matrix. That sounds restrictive because it is. It is also the most useful
approximation in navigation.

The chapter derives the filter from Gaussian conditioning, builds a complete
simulation you can poke at, and then spends real time on the parts that
separate a filter that *runs* from a filter that *works*: process-noise
modeling, consistency testing, and smoothing. @sec-ekf then relaxes the
linearity assumption.

## Linear Gaussian Systems {#sec-kf-linear-gaussian-systems}

The discrete-time linear system model is

$$
\mathbf{x}_k =
\mathbf{F}_k \mathbf{x}_{k-1}
+
\mathbf{B}_k \mathbf{u}_k
+
\mathbf{w}_k,
\qquad
\mathbf{w}_k \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{Q}_k),
$$ {#eq-kf-process-model}

with measurement model

$$
\mathbf{z}_k =
\mathbf{H}_k \mathbf{x}_k
+
\mathbf{v}_k,
\qquad
\mathbf{v}_k \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{R}_k).
$$ {#eq-kf-measurement-model}

The process noise $\mathbf{w}_k$ and measurement noise $\mathbf{v}_k$ are
zero-mean, white (uncorrelated across time), uncorrelated with each other, and
uncorrelated with the initial state. Each of those words is an assumption you
will eventually see violated by real hardware.

The symbols have standard roles. $\mathbf{F}_k$ propagates the state,
$\mathbf{B}_k$ maps known inputs into the state, $\mathbf{Q}_k$ describes
process noise and unmodeled dynamics, $\mathbf{H}_k$ maps state into
measurement space, and $\mathbf{R}_k$ describes measurement noise.

The belief is a Gaussian with a mean and covariance. The subscript $k|j$ reads
"the estimate at step $k$ using measurements through step $j$." In the language
of @sec-bayes,

$$
\operatorname{bel}(\mathbf{x}_{k-1})
=
\mathcal{N}\!\left(\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{k-1|k-1}, \mathbf{P}_{k-1|k-1}\right),
\qquad
\overline{\operatorname{bel}}(\mathbf{x}_{k})
=
\mathcal{N}\!\left(\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{k|k-1}, \mathbf{P}_{k|k-1}\right).
$$

The prior (predicted) estimate is $\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{k|k-1}$ and the posterior
(updated) estimate is $\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{k|k}$. If the assumptions hold, the
Kalman filter is not an approximation of the Bayes filter. It *is* the Bayes
filter, written in closed form.

## Prediction {#sec-kf-prediction}

The Bayes prediction integral pushes the previous belief through the
transition model. When the belief is Gaussian and the transition is linear with
additive Gaussian noise, the result is Gaussian with mean and covariance given
by the linear-transformation rule from @sec-filtering-why-linear-gaussian:

$$
\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{k|k-1}
=
\mathbf{F}_k \hat{\mathbf{x}}_{k-1|k-1}
+
\mathbf{B}_k \mathbf{u}_k,
$$ {#eq-kf-predict-mean}

$$
\mathbf{P}_{k|k-1}
=
\mathbf{F}_k \mathbf{P}_{k-1|k-1} \mathbf{F}_k^T
+
\mathbf{Q}_k.
$$ {#eq-kf-predict-cov}

The covariance equation says two things at once. First, existing uncertainty is
transformed by the dynamics: position uncertainty grows as velocity uncertainty
leaks into it. Second, new uncertainty enters through process noise. If
$\mathbf{Q}_k$ is too small, the filter becomes overconfident and may reject
valid measurements. If $\mathbf{Q}_k$ is too large, the filter wanders around
and lets measurements dominate. @sec-kf-process-noise shows how to build
$\mathbf{Q}_k$ from physics rather than from hope.

## Deriving the Update by Gaussian Conditioning {#sec-kf-derivation}

The measurement update is Bayes' rule. For Gaussians, Bayes' rule reduces to a
single piece of linear algebra: conditioning one block of a jointly Gaussian
vector on another. That is the whole derivation, so it is worth doing
carefully. The probability background is in @sec-probability and the matrix
background in @sec-linalg.

### Conditioning a Joint Gaussian {#sec-kf-conditioning-joint-gaussian}

Suppose two random vectors $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}$ are jointly Gaussian:

$$
\begin{bmatrix}
\mathbf{a} \\ \mathbf{b}
\end{bmatrix}
\sim
\mathcal{N}\!\left(
\begin{bmatrix}
\boldsymbol{\mu}_a \\ \boldsymbol{\mu}_b
\end{bmatrix},
\begin{bmatrix}
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{aa} & \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{ab} \\
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{ba} & \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{bb}
\end{bmatrix}
\right).
$$

Then $\mathbf{a}$ given an observed value of $\mathbf{b}$ is Gaussian with

$$
\mathbf{a} \mid \mathbf{b}
\sim
\mathcal{N}\!\left(
\boldsymbol{\mu}_a + \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{ab}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{bb}^{-1}(\mathbf{b} - \boldsymbol{\mu}_b),
\;
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{aa} - \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{ab}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{bb}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{ba}
\right).
$$ {#eq-kf-gaussian-conditioning}

Here is a proof that fits on an index card. Define the residual

$$
\mathbf{r}
=
\mathbf{a} - \boldsymbol{\mu}_a
- \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{ab}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{bb}^{-1}(\mathbf{b} - \boldsymbol{\mu}_b).
$$

It is a linear function of jointly Gaussian variables, so $\mathbf{r}$ and
$\mathbf{b}$ are jointly Gaussian. Their cross-covariance is

$$
\operatorname{Cov}(\mathbf{r}, \mathbf{b})
=
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{ab}
- \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{ab}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{bb}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{bb}
= \mathbf{0}.
$$

Uncorrelated jointly Gaussian variables are independent (this is the one place
where "Gaussian" does real work; see
@sec-probability-cross-covariance-independence). So learning $\mathbf{b}$ tells
us nothing about $\mathbf{r}$. Rearranging the definition,

$$
\mathbf{a}
=
\underbrace{\boldsymbol{\mu}_a + \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{ab}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{bb}^{-1}(\mathbf{b} - \boldsymbol{\mu}_b)}_{\text{known once } \mathbf{b} \text{ is observed}}
+
\underbrace{\mathbf{r}}_{\text{independent of } \mathbf{b}},
$$

and expanding $\operatorname{Cov}(\mathbf{r})$ gives
$\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{aa} - \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{ab}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{bb}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{ba}$.
That matrix is the **Schur complement** of $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{bb}$ in the
joint covariance. It also appears in the block inverse: the upper-left block of
the joint *information* matrix is exactly the inverse of this Schur complement,
which is why the information filter of @sec-information-filter can condition
by simply reading off a block.

### Reading Off the Kalman Filter {#sec-kf-reading-off-filter}

Now apply @eq-kf-gaussian-conditioning to the state and the measurement. Given
all measurements through $k-1$, the state is
$\mathcal{N}(\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{k|k-1}, \mathbf{P}_{k|k-1})$, and
$\mathbf{z}_k = \mathbf{H}_k\mathbf{x}_k + \mathbf{v}_k$ is a linear function of
the state and an independent Gaussian noise. The pair is therefore jointly
Gaussian:

$$
\begin{bmatrix}
\mathbf{x}_k \\ \mathbf{z}_k
\end{bmatrix}
\sim
\mathcal{N}\!\left(
\begin{bmatrix}
\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{k|k-1} \\
\mathbf{H}_k \hat{\mathbf{x}}_{k|k-1}
\end{bmatrix},
\begin{bmatrix}
\mathbf{P}_{k|k-1} & \mathbf{P}_{k|k-1}\mathbf{H}_k^T \\
\mathbf{H}_k\mathbf{P}_{k|k-1} & \mathbf{H}_k\mathbf{P}_{k|k-1}\mathbf{H}_k^T + \mathbf{R}_k
\end{bmatrix}
\right).
$$ {#eq-kf-joint}

Match the blocks: $\mathbf{a} = \mathbf{x}_k$, $\mathbf{b} = \mathbf{z}_k$,
$\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{ab} = \mathbf{P}_{k|k-1}\mathbf{H}_k^T$, and
$\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{bb} = \mathbf{H}_k\mathbf{P}_{k|k-1}\mathbf{H}_k^T + \mathbf{R}_k$.
Give the recurring pieces names:

$$
\boldsymbol{\nu}_k = \mathbf{z}_k - \mathbf{H}_k\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{k|k-1}
\quad \text{(innovation)},
\qquad
\mathbf{S}_k = \mathbf{H}_k\mathbf{P}_{k|k-1}\mathbf{H}_k^T + \mathbf{R}_k
\quad \text{(innovation covariance)},
$$

$$
\mathbf{K}_k = \mathbf{P}_{k|k-1}\mathbf{H}_k^T\mathbf{S}_k^{-1}
\quad \text{(Kalman gain)}.
$$

The conditional mean and covariance are then

$$
\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{k|k} = \hat{\mathbf{x}}_{k|k-1} + \mathbf{K}_k\boldsymbol{\nu}_k,
\qquad
\mathbf{P}_{k|k} = \mathbf{P}_{k|k-1} - \mathbf{K}_k\mathbf{S}_k\mathbf{K}_k^T
= (\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{K}_k\mathbf{H}_k)\mathbf{P}_{k|k-1}.
$$

That is the Kalman filter. No calculus of variations, no optimal control, just
"condition a Gaussian." Two consequences are worth pausing on.

First, $\mathbf{P}_{k|k}$ does not depend on the measured value $\mathbf{z}_k$,
only on $\mathbf{H}_k$, $\mathbf{R}_k$, and the prior. You can run the
covariance recursion *before* building the vehicle. This is covariance analysis,
and it is how navigation engineers decide whether a proposed sensor suite can
meet a requirement before anyone buys a sensor.

Second, the derivation has a non-Gaussian reading. Drop the Gaussian assumption
and keep only means and covariances, and the same gain still gives the
minimum-mean-square-error estimator among all *linear* estimators. Its defining
property is the orthogonality principle: the estimation error is uncorrelated
with the innovation and with every past measurement, which is precisely the
$\operatorname{Cov}(\mathbf{r}, \mathbf{b}) = \mathbf{0}$ statement above
[@barShalom2001].

Do not take the conditioning formula on faith. The cell below draws a million
samples of a scalar state and measurement, keeps only the samples whose
measurement landed near a particular value, and compares their statistics to the
Kalman update.

```{python}
#| label: kf-conditioning-check

import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(11)

x_prior, P_prior = 10.0, 4.0     # prior mean and variance of the state
R = 1.0                          # measurement noise variance
z_observed = 12.5                # the measurement we "received"

# Sample the joint distribution of (x, z) implied by the model.
x_samples = x_prior + np.sqrt(P_prior) * rng.standard_normal(1_000_000)
z_samples = x_samples + np.sqrt(R) * rng.standard_normal(x_samples.size)

# Brute-force conditioning: keep samples whose measurement is close to z_observed.
near = np.abs(z_samples - z_observed) < 0.02
x_given_z = x_samples[near]

# Kalman update for the same problem.
S = P_prior + R
K = P_prior / S
x_post = x_prior + K * (z_observed - x_prior)
P_post = (1.0 - K) * P_prior

print(f"samples kept:       {x_given_z.size}")
print(f"empirical mean/var: {x_given_z.mean():.3f} / {x_given_z.var():.3f}")
print(f"Kalman mean/var:    {x_post:.3f} / {P_post:.3f}")
```

## The Measurement Update {#sec-kf-measurement-update}

Collecting the results, one Kalman filter cycle is

$$
\begin{aligned}
\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{k|k-1} &= \mathbf{F}_k \hat{\mathbf{x}}_{k-1|k-1} + \mathbf{B}_k \mathbf{u}_k, \\
\mathbf{P}_{k|k-1} &= \mathbf{F}_k \mathbf{P}_{k-1|k-1} \mathbf{F}_k^T + \mathbf{Q}_k, \\
\boldsymbol{\nu}_k &= \mathbf{z}_k - \mathbf{H}_k \hat{\mathbf{x}}_{k|k-1}, \\
\mathbf{S}_k &= \mathbf{H}_k \mathbf{P}_{k|k-1} \mathbf{H}_k^T + \mathbf{R}_k, \\
\mathbf{K}_k &= \mathbf{P}_{k|k-1} \mathbf{H}_k^T \mathbf{S}_k^{-1}, \\
\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{k|k} &= \hat{\mathbf{x}}_{k|k-1} + \mathbf{K}_k \boldsymbol{\nu}_k, \\
\mathbf{P}_{k|k} &= (\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{K}_k \mathbf{H}_k)\mathbf{P}_{k|k-1}(\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{K}_k \mathbf{H}_k)^T + \mathbf{K}_k \mathbf{R}_k \mathbf{K}_k^T.
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-kf-cycle}

The last line is the Joseph form of the covariance update, explained in
@sec-kf-joseph-form. The implementation follows the equations directly. Two
habits are worth building from day one: solve a linear system for the gain
instead of forming $\mathbf{S}_k^{-1}$, and return the innovation and its
covariance so you can test the filter later.

```{python}
#| label: kf-core-functions

import numpy as np


def kf_predict(x, P, F, Q, B=None, u=None):
    """Kalman prediction: returns the prior mean and covariance.

    x, P : posterior mean (n,) and covariance (n, n) at step k-1
    F, Q : state transition (n, n) and process-noise covariance (n, n)
    B, u : optional input matrix (n, p) and known input (p,)
    """
    x_pred = F @ x if B is None else F @ x + B @ u
    P_pred = F @ P @ F.T + Q
    return x_pred, P_pred


def kf_update(x_pred, P_pred, z, H, R):
    """Kalman measurement update with the Joseph covariance form.

    Returns the posterior mean and covariance plus the innovation and its
    covariance, which are needed for consistency checks.
    """
    nu = z - H @ x_pred                       # innovation
    S = H @ P_pred @ H.T + R                  # innovation covariance
    # K = P H^T S^{-1}. Since P and S are symmetric, K^T = S^{-1} H P,
    # so a single linear solve gives the gain without inverting S.
    K = np.linalg.solve(S, H @ P_pred).T
    x_post = x_pred + K @ nu
    I_KH = np.eye(x_pred.size) - K @ H
    P_post = I_KH @ P_pred @ I_KH.T + K @ R @ K.T
    return x_post, P_post, nu, S
```

When $\mathbf{R}_k$ is diagonal, the measurement components are independent and
can be processed one scalar at a time, each update using the previous one's
output as its prior. Each step then needs only a scalar division, and the result
is identical to the batch update. Many flight codes are written this way.

## The Joseph Form and Factored Filters {#sec-kf-joseph-form}

Where does the Joseph form come from, and why do we prefer it? Write the
posterior error for an arbitrary gain $\mathbf{K}$ (errors are true minus
estimate):

$$
\mathbf{e}_{k|k}
=
\mathbf{x}_k - \hat{\mathbf{x}}_{k|k}
=
\mathbf{x}_k - \hat{\mathbf{x}}_{k|k-1} - \mathbf{K}(\mathbf{H}_k\mathbf{x}_k + \mathbf{v}_k - \mathbf{H}_k\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{k|k-1})
=
(\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{K}\mathbf{H}_k)\mathbf{e}_{k|k-1} - \mathbf{K}\mathbf{v}_k.
$$

The prior error and the new measurement noise are uncorrelated, so

$$
\mathbf{P}_{k|k}
=
(\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{K}\mathbf{H}_k)\mathbf{P}_{k|k-1}(\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{K}\mathbf{H}_k)^T
+ \mathbf{K}\mathbf{R}_k\mathbf{K}^T.
$$ {#eq-kf-joseph}

Nothing in that derivation used the optimal gain. **The Joseph form is the
correct covariance for any gain**, optimal or not. The short form
$(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{K}\mathbf{H})\mathbf{P}_{k|k-1}$ is what you get after
substituting the optimal gain, so it is only correct when the gain is exactly
optimal. Real filters use suboptimal gains all the time: a measurement that is
deweighted because it looked suspicious, a gated update, a precomputed
steady-state gain, a reduced-order filter that ignores some states, or a gain
computed in slightly different arithmetic than the covariance. In all of these
cases only the Joseph form tells the truth.

It is also better numerically. The Joseph form is a congruence of a
positive-semidefinite matrix plus another positive-semidefinite matrix, so
roundoff cannot easily make it indefinite. The short form subtracts, and
subtraction is how covariances acquire negative eigenvalues after a few hours of
flight. The cell below uses a deliberately halved gain and checks both formulas
against Monte Carlo.

```{python}
#| label: kf-joseph-check

import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(5)

P_prior = np.array([[4.0, 1.0], [1.0, 2.0]])
H = np.array([[1.0, 0.0]])
R = np.array([[1.0]])

S = H @ P_prior @ H.T + R
K_opt = np.linalg.solve(S, H @ P_prior).T
K_sub = 0.5 * K_opt                      # e.g. a deweighted, suspicious measurement

I_KH = np.eye(2) - K_sub @ H
P_joseph = I_KH @ P_prior @ I_KH.T + K_sub @ R @ K_sub.T
P_short = I_KH @ P_prior                 # only valid for the optimal gain

# Monte Carlo: e+ = (I - K H) e- - K v
e_prior = rng.multivariate_normal(np.zeros(2), P_prior, size=200_000)
v = rng.normal(0.0, np.sqrt(R[0, 0]), size=(200_000, 1))
e_post = e_prior @ I_KH.T - v @ K_sub.T
P_monte_carlo = np.cov(e_post.T)

np.set_printoptions(precision=3, suppress=True)
print("Monte Carlo:\n", P_monte_carlo)
print("Joseph form:\n", P_joseph)
print("short form (wrong for this gain):\n", P_short)
```

Even the Joseph form has limits. An inertial navigation filter may carry
position errors of meters next to gyro biases of $10^{-6}$ rad/s, so the
covariance eigenvalues can span more than twelve orders of magnitude.
**Square-root filters** propagate a factor $\mathbf{P} = \mathbf{L}\mathbf{L}^T$
instead of $\mathbf{P}$ itself; the factor's condition number is the square root
of the covariance's, which effectively doubles the available precision and
guarantees a positive-semidefinite result. Bierman's **UD filter** factors
$\mathbf{P} = \mathbf{U}\mathbf{D}\mathbf{U}^T$ with $\mathbf{U}$ unit upper
triangular and $\mathbf{D}$ diagonal, and processes scalar measurements without
any square roots [@bierman1977]. UD filters flew on 1970s and 1980s flight
computers with short word lengths and are still common in spacecraft navigation.
For coursework with 64-bit floats and well-scaled states, Joseph plus an
occasional symmetrization is usually enough. When a long-duration INS filter's
covariance goes indefinite, factored forms are the grown-up fix.

## Kalman Gain Intuition {#sec-kf-gain-intuition}

In a scalar measurement problem with $H = 1$, the gain is

$$
K = \frac{P_{k|k-1}}{P_{k|k-1} + R}.
$$

If measurement noise $R$ is small, $K$ approaches one and the filter trusts the
measurement. If $R$ is large, $K$ approaches zero and the filter trusts the
prediction. The matrix gain
$\mathbf{K} = \mathbf{P}_{k|k-1}\mathbf{H}^T\mathbf{S}^{-1}$ is the same ratio
in disguise: the prior uncertainty mapped into measurement space, divided by the
total uncertainty of the innovation. The off-diagonal terms of
$\mathbf{P}_{k|k-1}\mathbf{H}^T$ are what let a position measurement correct a
velocity it never saw.

```{python}
#| label: fig-kf-gain-noise
#| fig-cap: "Scalar Kalman gain as measurement noise changes. Larger predicted uncertainty increases measurement influence; larger measurement noise decreases it."
#| code-fold: true

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

R_values = np.logspace(-3, 2, 500)
predicted_variances = [0.05, 0.2, 1.0, 5.0]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4))
for P_pred in predicted_variances:
    gain = P_pred / (P_pred + R_values)
    ax.semilogx(R_values, gain, label=fr"$P_{{k|k-1}}={P_pred}$")

ax.set_xlabel("measurement variance R")
ax.set_ylabel("Kalman gain K")
ax.set_title("Measurement trust decreases as measurement noise increases")
ax.grid(True, which="both", alpha=0.25)
ax.legend()
plt.show()
```

The gain is not a magic tuning knob. It is the consequence of the uncertainty
model. If the gain seems wrong, inspect $\mathbf{P}_{k|k-1}$ and $\mathbf{R}$
before you start sprinkling constants into the code.

## A Constant-Velocity Example {#sec-kf-cv-example}

Time to run one. A survey vessel transits a dredged channel at roughly constant
speed. Its GNSS receiver reports along-track position once per second with a
standard deviation of 4 m, and we want position and speed. The state is
along-track position $s$ and speed $\dot{s}$:

$$
\mathbf{x}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
s \\
\dot{s}
\end{bmatrix},
\qquad
\mathbf{F}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
1 & \Delta t \\
0 & 1
\end{bmatrix},
\qquad
\mathbf{H}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
1 & 0
\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Nobody holds a ship's speed perfectly constant: currents, wind, and the
helmsman all perturb it. We model those perturbations as white-noise
acceleration with power spectral density $q$, which gives the process-noise
matrix derived in @sec-kf-process-noise:

$$
\mathbf{Q}
=
q
\begin{bmatrix}
\Delta t^3/3 & \Delta t^2/2 \\
\Delta t^2/2 & \Delta t
\end{bmatrix}.
$$

The simulation generates the truth from exactly this model, so the filter's
assumptions are correct. That is the right place to start: if a filter misbehaves
when its model is *perfect*, the bug is in the code, not the physics.

```{python}
#| label: kf-cv-simulation

import numpy as np


def cv_model(dt, q):
    """Constant-velocity transition and continuous white-noise-acceleration Q."""
    F = np.array([[1.0, dt],
                  [0.0, 1.0]])
    Q = q * np.array([[dt**3 / 3.0, dt**2 / 2.0],
                      [dt**2 / 2.0, dt]])
    return F, Q


def simulate_cv(rng, n_steps, dt, q, sigma_z, x0):
    """Simulate truth and position measurements. Index 0 is the initial state."""
    F, Q = cv_model(dt, q)
    L_Q = np.linalg.cholesky(Q)             # w_k = L_Q @ n with n ~ N(0, I)
    x_true = np.zeros((n_steps + 1, 2))
    x_true[0] = x0
    z = np.full((n_steps + 1, 1), np.nan)   # no measurement at k = 0
    for k in range(1, n_steps + 1):
        x_true[k] = F @ x_true[k - 1] + L_Q @ rng.standard_normal(2)
        z[k, 0] = x_true[k, 0] + sigma_z * rng.standard_normal()
    return x_true, z


def run_kf(z, F, Q, H, R, x0_hat, P0):
    """Run a linear KF over z[1:], storing priors (for smoothing) and innovations."""
    n_steps, n, m = len(z) - 1, x0_hat.size, H.shape[0]
    out = {
        "x": np.zeros((n_steps + 1, n)), "P": np.zeros((n_steps + 1, n, n)),
        "x_pred": np.zeros((n_steps + 1, n)), "P_pred": np.zeros((n_steps + 1, n, n)),
        "nu": np.zeros((n_steps + 1, m)), "S": np.zeros((n_steps + 1, m, m)),
    }
    out["x"][0], out["P"][0] = x0_hat, P0
    out["x_pred"][0], out["P_pred"][0] = x0_hat, P0
    for k in range(1, n_steps + 1):
        x_pred, P_pred = kf_predict(out["x"][k - 1], out["P"][k - 1], F, Q)
        x_post, P_post, nu, S = kf_update(x_pred, P_pred, z[k], H, R)
        out["x_pred"][k], out["P_pred"][k] = x_pred, P_pred
        out["x"][k], out["P"][k] = x_post, P_post
        out["nu"][k], out["S"][k] = nu, S
    return out


# Scenario: 1 Hz GNSS, 4 m noise, ship near 5 m/s.
dt, q_true, sigma_z, n_steps = 1.0, 0.1, 4.0, 150
H = np.array([[1.0, 0.0]])
R = np.array([[sigma_z**2]])
x0_true = np.array([0.0, 5.0])
P0 = np.diag([10.0**2, 2.0**2])

rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
x_true, z = simulate_cv(rng, n_steps, dt, q_true, sigma_z, x0_true)
# Draw the initial estimate so that its error really has covariance P0.
x0_hat = x0_true + np.linalg.cholesky(P0) @ rng.standard_normal(2)

F, Q = cv_model(dt, q_true)
kf = run_kf(z, F, Q, H, R, x0_hat, P0)

err = x_true - kf["x"]
sigma = np.sqrt(np.stack([kf["P"][:, 0, 0], kf["P"][:, 1, 1]], axis=1))
print(f"raw GNSS position RMSE: {np.sqrt(np.mean((z[1:, 0] - x_true[1:, 0])**2)):.2f} m")
print(f"KF position RMSE:       {np.sqrt(np.mean(err[1:, 0]**2)):.2f} m")
print(f"KF speed RMSE:          {np.sqrt(np.mean(err[1:, 1]**2)):.2f} m/s")
print(f"fraction of errors inside 3 sigma (pos, vel): "
      f"{np.mean(np.abs(err[1:]) < 3 * sigma[1:], axis=0)}")
```

The filter cuts the position error of the raw fixes by more than 40% and
recovers a speed the sensor never measured. @fig-kf-cv-truth compares truth and estimate
directly. The position panel zooms in on the first minute, because at full scale
a 4 m error on a 750 m track is invisible.

```{python}
#| label: fig-kf-cv-truth
#| fig-cap: "Constant-velocity Kalman filter on simulated GNSS fixes. Top: the first 60 s of along-track position. Bottom: estimated speed with its ±3σ band against the true speed, which the sensor never measures directly."
#| code-fold: true

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

t = np.arange(n_steps + 1) * dt
window = t <= 60.0

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(8, 6.5))
ax = axes[0]
ax.plot(t[window], x_true[window, 0], color="k", label="truth")
ax.plot(t[window], z[window, 0], ".", color="C1", alpha=0.7, label="GNSS fixes")
ax.plot(t[window], kf["x"][window, 0], color="C0", label="KF estimate")
ax.set_ylabel("along-track position [m]")
ax.legend()
ax.grid(True, alpha=0.25)

ax = axes[1]
ax.fill_between(t, kf["x"][:, 1] - 3 * sigma[:, 1], kf["x"][:, 1] + 3 * sigma[:, 1],
                color="C0", alpha=0.2, label=r"estimate $\pm 3\sigma$")
ax.plot(t, x_true[:, 1], color="k", label="true speed")
ax.plot(t, kf["x"][:, 1], color="C0", label="KF speed")
ax.set_ylim(0.0, 10.0)
ax.set_xlabel("time [s]")
ax.set_ylabel("speed [m/s]")
ax.legend(loc="upper right")
ax.grid(True, alpha=0.25)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

The more useful plot is the error plot, @fig-kf-cv-errors. In simulation we know
the truth, so we can check whether the errors actually stay inside the bounds the
filter claims. The third panel shows the innovations, which is the one diagnostic
you can also compute on a real vehicle with no truth at all. For a healthy filter
they hover around zero, about 99.7% of them fall inside $\pm 3\sqrt{S_k}$, and
they look like structureless noise.

```{python}
#| label: fig-kf-cv-errors
#| fig-cap: "Estimation errors with the filter's ±3σ bounds (top two panels) and innovations with ±3√S bounds (bottom). Errors stay inside the bounds and the innovations look white, as they should when the model is correct."
#| code-fold: true

fig, axes = plt.subplots(3, 1, figsize=(8, 7.5), sharex=True)
labels = ["position error [m]", "speed error [m/s]"]
for i, ax in enumerate(axes[:2]):
    ax.plot(t, err[:, i], color="C0", label="error (true - estimate)")
    ax.plot(t, 3 * sigma[:, i], "--", color="C3", label=r"$\pm 3\sigma$")
    ax.plot(t, -3 * sigma[:, i], "--", color="C3")
    ax.set_ylabel(labels[i])
    ax.grid(True, alpha=0.25)
axes[0].set_ylim(-15, 15)
axes[1].set_ylim(-4, 4)
axes[0].legend(loc="upper right")

ax = axes[2]
s_nu = np.sqrt(kf["S"][1:, 0, 0])
ax.plot(t[1:], kf["nu"][1:, 0], ".", color="C2", label="innovation")
ax.plot(t[1:], 3 * s_nu, "--", color="C3", label=r"$\pm 3\sqrt{S_k}$")
ax.plot(t[1:], -3 * s_nu, "--", color="C3")
ax.set_ylabel("innovation [m]")
ax.set_xlabel("time [s]")
ax.legend(loc="upper right")
ax.grid(True, alpha=0.25)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

Notice how quickly the bounds settle. With a time-invariant model the gain and
covariance converge to steady-state values within a few dozen steps, and they
would converge to the same values for *any* measurement sequence, because, as
@sec-kf-derivation showed, the covariance recursion never looks at the data.

## Process Noise and Discretization {#sec-kf-process-noise}

$\mathbf{Q}$ is the most abused matrix in navigation. It is tempting to treat it
as "a small diagonal matrix because the code needed one." It is better treated
as a physical model of everything that pushes the state around that the
deterministic model leaves out. This section builds $\mathbf{Q}$ from a
continuous-time model, which is where the physics lives.

### Continuous Models {#sec-kf-continuous-models}

Real motion is continuous; digital filters run at discrete steps. A common
continuous-time linear model is

$$
\dot{\mathbf{x}}(t)
=
\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}(t)
+
\mathbf{B}\mathbf{u}(t)
+
\mathbf{G}\mathbf{w}(t),
\qquad
\mathbb{E}\!\left[\mathbf{w}(t)\mathbf{w}(\tau)^T\right] = \mathbf{Q}_c\,\delta(t - \tau),
$$

where $\mathbf{w}(t)$ is continuous white noise, $\mathbf{G}$ says which states
it drives, and $\mathbf{Q}_c$ is its **power spectral density**. Note the units:
if $w$ is an acceleration in m/s², then $\mathbf{Q}_c$ has units of
(m/s²)²·s = m²/s³. It is a density, not a variance, which is exactly what a
sensor data sheet gives you when it quotes noise in units per $\sqrt{\text{Hz}}$.

Over one step $\Delta t$ the state transition is the matrix exponential
$\boldsymbol{\Phi} = e^{\mathbf{A}\Delta t}$ (approximately
$\mathbf{I} + \mathbf{A}\Delta t$ for small steps), and the discrete process
noise accumulates every bit of white noise injected during the interval,
propagated to the end of it:

$$
\mathbf{Q}_d
=
\int_0^{\Delta t}
\boldsymbol{\Phi}(\tau)\,\mathbf{G}\mathbf{Q}_c\mathbf{G}^T\,\boldsymbol{\Phi}(\tau)^T
\,d\tau,
\qquad
\boldsymbol{\Phi}(\tau) = e^{\mathbf{A}\tau}.
$$ {#eq-kf-qd-integral}

### White-Noise Acceleration Models {#sec-kf-white-noise-acceleration}

For the constant-velocity model,

$$
\mathbf{A}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
0 & 1 \\
0 & 0
\end{bmatrix},
\qquad
\mathbf{G}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
0 \\ 1
\end{bmatrix},
\qquad
\boldsymbol{\Phi}(\tau)
=
\begin{bmatrix}
1 & \tau \\
0 & 1
\end{bmatrix},
\qquad
\boldsymbol{\Phi}(\tau)\mathbf{G}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
\tau \\ 1
\end{bmatrix}.
$$

With scalar spectral density $Q_c = q$, @eq-kf-qd-integral becomes an integral
of polynomials:

$$
\mathbf{Q}_d
=
q\int_0^{\Delta t}
\begin{bmatrix}
\tau^2 & \tau \\
\tau & 1
\end{bmatrix}
d\tau
=
q
\begin{bmatrix}
\Delta t^3/3 & \Delta t^2/2 \\
\Delta t^2/2 & \Delta t
\end{bmatrix}.
$$ {#eq-kf-cwna}

This is the **continuous white-noise acceleration** (CWNA) model. Its matrix is
full rank, and it scales correctly when you change the step size: run the filter
at 10 Hz or 100 Hz with the same $q$ and the accumulated uncertainty over one
second is the same.

A different and also common model assumes the acceleration is a random constant
over each step, independent from step to step, with variance $\sigma_a^2$. The
acceleration enters through $\mathbf{G}_d = [\Delta t^2/2, \; \Delta t]^T$, so

$$
\mathbf{Q}_d
=
\mathbf{G}_d\sigma_a^2\mathbf{G}_d^T
=
\sigma_a^2
\begin{bmatrix}
\Delta t^4/4 & \Delta t^3/2 \\
\Delta t^3/2 & \Delta t^2
\end{bmatrix}.
$$ {#eq-kf-pwca}

This **piecewise-constant acceleration** model has rank one, its parameter
$\sigma_a^2$ has units of m²/s⁴ rather than m²/s³, and it is tied to the step
size. Neither model is "right." CWNA describes a platform buffeted continuously
by many small forces, like a ship in a seaway. Piecewise-constant acceleration
fits a vehicle whose commanded acceleration genuinely changes once per control
cycle. What is wrong is plugging a $\sigma_a^2$ into the CWNA matrix or vice
versa: the units do not match, and the filter will be mistuned by a factor that
depends on $\Delta t$. A useful starting point for CWNA is to choose $q$ so that
$\sqrt{q\,\Delta t}$ is about the speed change you expect over one step; for the
piecewise model, $\sigma_a$ between one half and one times the largest expected
acceleration [@barShalom2001].

### The Van Loan Method {#sec-kf-van-loan}

@eq-kf-qd-integral is easy for the constant-velocity model and tedious for
almost anything else. Van Loan's method computes $\boldsymbol{\Phi}$ and
$\mathbf{Q}_d$ together from one matrix exponential [@vanLoan1978]. Build the
$2n \times 2n$ block matrix

$$
\mathbf{M}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
-\mathbf{A} & \mathbf{G}\mathbf{Q}_c\mathbf{G}^T \\
\mathbf{0} & \mathbf{A}^T
\end{bmatrix}\Delta t,
\qquad
e^{\mathbf{M}}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
\cdots & \boldsymbol{\Phi}^{-1}\mathbf{Q}_d \\
\mathbf{0} & \boldsymbol{\Phi}^T
\end{bmatrix}.
$$

The lower-right block is $\boldsymbol{\Phi}^T$, and premultiplying the
upper-right block by $\boldsymbol{\Phi}$ gives $\mathbf{Q}_d$. The cell checks
the method against @eq-kf-cwna and then uses it on a model where nobody wants to
do the integral by hand: a vessel whose speed perturbations decay with a drag
time constant $\tau_d$, so $\dot{v} = -v/\tau_d + w$. A numerical quadrature of
@eq-kf-qd-integral serves as an independent check.

```{python}
#| label: kf-van-loan

import numpy as np
from scipy.integrate import quad_vec
from scipy.linalg import expm


def van_loan(A, G, Qc, dt):
    """Discretize (A, G, Qc) over dt. Returns Phi and Q_d."""
    n = A.shape[0]
    M = np.zeros((2 * n, 2 * n))
    M[:n, :n] = -A
    M[:n, n:] = G @ Qc @ G.T
    M[n:, n:] = A.T
    E = expm(M * dt)
    Phi = E[n:, n:].T
    Q_d = Phi @ E[:n, n:]
    return Phi, 0.5 * (Q_d + Q_d.T)   # symmetrize away roundoff


q, dt_vl = 0.1, 0.5
A_cv = np.array([[0.0, 1.0], [0.0, 0.0]])
G_cv = np.array([[0.0], [1.0]])
Phi, Q_d = van_loan(A_cv, G_cv, np.array([[q]]), dt_vl)
F_closed, Q_closed = cv_model(dt_vl, q)
print("CV model: Van Loan matches closed form:",
      np.allclose(Phi, F_closed) and np.allclose(Q_d, Q_closed))

# Speed perturbations with first-order drag: v_dot = -v / tau_d + w.
tau_d = 20.0
A_drag = np.array([[0.0, 1.0], [0.0, -1.0 / tau_d]])
Phi_drag, Q_drag = van_loan(A_drag, G_cv, np.array([[q]]), dt_vl)


def integrand(tau):
    PhiG = expm(A_drag * tau) @ G_cv
    return (PhiG * q) @ PhiG.T


Q_quad, _ = quad_vec(integrand, 0.0, dt_vl)
np.set_printoptions(precision=6, suppress=True)
print("drag model Q_d (Van Loan):\n", Q_drag)
print("matches numerical quadrature:", np.allclose(Q_drag, Q_quad, rtol=1e-8, atol=1e-12))
```

### Noise That Enters Through Inputs {#sec-kf-input-noise}

Often the noisiest thing in the propagation is not an unknown force but a
*measured input*. Suppose the filter knows the input $\mathbf{u}_k$ only through
a sensor, so the input the vehicle actually experienced was
$\mathbf{u}_k + \mathbf{n}_k$ with
$\mathbf{n}_k \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{Q}_u)$. Then

$$
\mathbf{x}_k
=
\mathbf{F}_k\mathbf{x}_{k-1} + \mathbf{B}_k(\mathbf{u}_k + \mathbf{n}_k),
$$

and the input noise appears as process noise
$\mathbf{w}_k = \mathbf{B}_k\mathbf{n}_k$ with covariance
$\mathbf{B}_k\mathbf{Q}_u\mathbf{B}_k^T$. For a nonlinear model
$\mathbf{x}_k = f(\mathbf{x}_{k-1}, \mathbf{u}_k + \mathbf{n}_k)$, the same
argument with the input Jacobian $\mathbf{L}_k = \partial f / \partial \mathbf{u}$
gives

$$
\mathbf{P}_{k|k-1}
=
\mathbf{F}_k\mathbf{P}_{k-1|k-1}\mathbf{F}_k^T
+
\mathbf{L}_k\mathbf{Q}_u\mathbf{L}_k^T.
$$ {#eq-kf-input-noise}

If the model has unmodeled dynamics beyond the noisy inputs, add a
$\mathbf{Q}_k$ term for them as well.

Thrun, Burgard, and Fox write the same thing as
$\mathbf{G}_t\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{t-1}\mathbf{G}_t^T + \mathbf{V}_t\mathbf{M}_t\mathbf{V}_t^T$,
where $\mathbf{V}_t$ is the control Jacobian and $\mathbf{M}_t$ the control-noise
covariance [@ProbRob]. In our constant-velocity model with a measured
acceleration held over the step, $\mathbf{L} = \mathbf{B} = [\Delta t^2/2,\;\Delta t]^T$
and $\mathbf{L}\mathbf{Q}_u\mathbf{L}^T$ is exactly @eq-kf-pwca. The
piecewise-constant acceleration model is literally "the acceleration input is
noisy and held over the step."

An inertial navigation system is the extreme case of this pattern. The
accelerometers and gyroscopes are *inputs* to the mechanization, not
measurements, and their noise densities enter the filter through
$\mathbf{L}\mathbf{Q}_u\mathbf{L}^T$ and @eq-kf-qd-integral. The INS chapters
build $\mathbf{Q}$ in exactly this way from data-sheet numbers (@sec-ins-errors,
especially @sec-ins-errors-from-imu-specs), and @sec-ekf uses the same input-noise
form for a wheeled robot.

## Observability {#sec-kf-observability}

A Kalman filter can only estimate what the measurements, combined with the
dynamics, actually reveal. For a time-invariant system with $n$ states, stack
the measurement matrix propagated through the dynamics:

$$
\mathcal{O}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
\mathbf{H} \\
\mathbf{H}\mathbf{F} \\
\vdots \\
\mathbf{H}\mathbf{F}^{n-1}
\end{bmatrix}.
$$

The system is observable if and only if $\mathcal{O}$ has rank $n$. Directions
in the null space of $\mathcal{O}$ are invisible to the sensors: their
covariance never shrinks, and a filter that claims otherwise is lying. For the
constant-velocity model, a position measurement makes both states observable
because speed shows up in how position changes. A speed-only measurement, like a
Doppler velocity log on an underwater vehicle, leaves position unobservable no
matter how long you wait.

```{python}
#| label: kf-observability

import numpy as np


def observability_matrix(F, H):
    n = F.shape[0]
    return np.vstack([H @ np.linalg.matrix_power(F, i) for i in range(n)])


F_cv = np.array([[1.0, 1.0], [0.0, 1.0]])
for name, H_test in [("position fix", np.array([[1.0, 0.0]])),
                     ("speed only (DVL)", np.array([[0.0, 1.0]]))]:
    rank = np.linalg.matrix_rank(observability_matrix(F_cv, H_test))
    print(f"{name:18s} rank {rank} of {F_cv.shape[0]}")
```

The rank test is binary; real systems are often *weakly* observable, and the
covariance tells you how weakly. For time-varying systems the observability of a
state can depend on the trajectory. In loosely coupled INS/GNSS, heading error
becomes observable only when the vehicle accelerates or turns
(@sec-ins-errors-observability-loose-ins). @sec-ins-errors returns to this when
choosing which error states to carry.

## Filter Consistency: NEES, NIS, and Tuning {#sec-kf-consistency}

A filter is **consistent** when its errors are zero-mean and its covariance
matches their actual spread: $\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{e}_k] = \mathbf{0}$ and
$\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{e}_k\mathbf{e}_k^T] = \mathbf{P}_{k|k}$. Accuracy and
consistency are different properties. A filter with 2 m errors that claims 2 m
is healthy. A filter with 1 m errors that claims 10 cm is a hazard: it will
reject good measurements, gate out correct data associations, and report
integrity it does not have. This section gives the standard tests, following
Bar-Shalom, Li, and Kirubarajan [@barShalom2001].

### NEES and NIS {#sec-kf-nees-nis}

The **normalized estimation error squared** uses the true error
$\mathbf{e}_k = \mathbf{x}_k - \hat{\mathbf{x}}_{k|k}$:

$$
\epsilon_k = \mathbf{e}_k^T\mathbf{P}_{k|k}^{-1}\mathbf{e}_k.
$$ {#eq-kf-nees}

If the filter is consistent and Gaussian, $\epsilon_k$ is chi-square distributed
with $n$ degrees of freedom, where $n$ is the state dimension, so its mean is
$n$. NEES needs the truth, which means simulation, a motion-capture reference
like the Vicon data in Project 1, or a post-processed reference trajectory.

The **normalized innovation squared** needs no truth:

$$
\epsilon_{\nu,k} = \boldsymbol{\nu}_k^T\mathbf{S}_k^{-1}\boldsymbol{\nu}_k,
$$ {#eq-kf-nis}

which is chi-square with $m$ degrees of freedom, $m$ being the measurement
dimension. You can compute it on the vehicle, in real time, and it is the basis
of measurement gating (@sec-slam-association-innovation-mahalanobis-distance).

A single sample of either statistic tells you little, because a chi-square
variable with a few degrees of freedom has a long tail. Average them. With $M$
independent Monte Carlo runs, the **average NEES** at step $k$ is

$$
\bar{\epsilon}_k = \frac{1}{M}\sum_{i=1}^{M}\epsilon_k^{(i)},
\qquad
M\bar{\epsilon}_k \sim \chi^2_{Mn}.
$$ {#eq-kf-anees}

For a two-sided test at 95%, the consistent region is

$$
\bar{\epsilon}_k \in
\left[
\frac{\chi^2_{Mn}(0.025)}{M},\;
\frac{\chi^2_{Mn}(0.975)}{M}
\right],
$$

where $\chi^2_{d}(p)$ is the $p$ quantile, `scipy.stats.chi2.ppf(p, d)`. The
average NIS (ANIS) works the same way with $m$ in place of $n$. On a single real
data set you cannot rerun the experiment, so average over time instead: with
$K$ updates, $K\bar{\epsilon}_\nu \sim \chi^2_{Km}$. That time-averaged NIS
compared to $m$ with these bounds is exactly the check Project 1 Part C asks for,
with $m = 6$ (@sec-project1c).

```{python}
#| label: kf-chi2-bounds

from scipy.stats import chi2


def chi2_bounds(dof_per_sample, n_samples, confidence=0.95):
    """Two-sided bounds on the average of n_samples chi-square(dof) variables."""
    alpha = 1.0 - confidence
    total_dof = dof_per_sample * n_samples
    lo, hi = chi2.ppf([alpha / 2.0, 1.0 - alpha / 2.0], total_dof)
    return lo / n_samples, hi / n_samples


print("ANEES, n = 2, M = 50 runs:      [%.2f, %.2f]" % chi2_bounds(2, 50))
print("time-avg NIS, m = 6, K = 1000:  [%.2f, %.2f]" % chi2_bounds(6, 1000))
```

### Innovation Whiteness {#sec-kf-whiteness}

The orthogonality principle has a second testable consequence: the innovations
of an optimal filter are white. Each innovation is the genuinely new part of its
measurement, so it should be uncorrelated with every earlier innovation. For a
scalar innovation sequence (or one component of a vector one), the sample
autocorrelation at lag $j$ is

$$
\hat{\rho}(j)
=
\frac{\sum_k \nu_k\nu_{k+j}}
{\sqrt{\sum_k \nu_k^2\,\sum_k \nu_{k+j}^2}},
$$

and for a white sequence of length $K$ it is approximately
$\mathcal{N}(0, 1/K)$, giving 95% bounds of $\pm 1.96/\sqrt{K}$. Correlated
innovations mean the filter is leaving information on the table: something
predictable is showing up in what the filter thinks is new.

### Reading the Diagnostics {#sec-kf-reading-diagnostics}

The interpretation is the part people get backwards, so here it is plainly. If
the average NEES or NIS is much **larger** than the dimension, the actual errors
are bigger than the filter believes: the filter is **overconfident**, with
$\mathbf{P}$ (or $\mathbf{S}$) too small. If it is much **smaller**, the filter
is **underconfident**, with $\mathbf{P}$ too large, which is safer but wastes
information.

NIS alone cannot tell you whether $\mathbf{Q}$ or $\mathbf{R}$ is to blame,
because both feed $\mathbf{S}$. Whiteness breaks the tie. A filter whose gain is
too low lags behind the truth, so consecutive innovations share the same sign
and the lag-one correlation is positive. A filter whose gain is too high chases
measurement noise, so consecutive innovations tend to alternate and the
correlation is negative. Combining the two gives a diagnostic table you can
verify with the simulation (Exercise 4):

| Mistake | Average NIS | Lag-one innovation correlation |
|---|---|---|
| $\mathbf{Q}$ too small | above $m$ | positive (filter lags) |
| $\mathbf{R}$ too small | above $m$ | negative (filter chases noise) |
| $\mathbf{Q}$ too large | below $m$ | negative (filter chases noise) |
| $\mathbf{R}$ too large | below $m$ | positive (filter lags) |

The Monte Carlo experiment below runs the vessel filter 50 times with the
correct $q$, a $q$ fifty times too small, and a $q$ fifty times too large, all
against the same truth model.

```{python}
#| label: kf-monte-carlo-consistency

import numpy as np


def normalized_squares(e, P):
    """e_k^T P_k^{-1} e_k for stacked e (N, d) and P (N, d, d)."""
    return np.einsum("ki,ki->k", e, np.linalg.solve(P, e[..., None])[..., 0])


def autocorrelation(x, max_lag):
    return np.array([np.sum(x[:-j] * x[j:]) / np.sqrt(np.sum(x[:-j]**2) * np.sum(x[j:]**2))
                     for j in range(1, max_lag + 1)])


n_runs, max_lag = 50, 15
q_cases = {"correct q": q_true, "q / 50 (too small)": q_true / 50, "q x 50 (too large)": q_true * 50}
mc = {}
for label, q_filter in q_cases.items():
    F_f, Q_f = cv_model(dt, q_filter)
    rng_mc = np.random.default_rng(7)            # same truth sequences for every case
    nees, nis = np.zeros((n_runs, n_steps)), np.zeros((n_runs, n_steps))
    for i in range(n_runs):
        x_t, z_i = simulate_cv(rng_mc, n_steps, dt, q_true, sigma_z, x0_true)
        x0_i = x0_true + np.linalg.cholesky(P0) @ rng_mc.standard_normal(2)
        run = run_kf(z_i, F_f, Q_f, H, R, x0_i, P0)
        nees[i] = normalized_squares((x_t - run["x"])[1:], run["P"][1:])
        nis[i] = normalized_squares(run["nu"][1:], run["S"][1:])
        if i == 0:   # whiteness from one run, as you would have on real data
            rho = autocorrelation(run["nu"][1:, 0], max_lag)
    mc[label] = {"anees": nees.mean(axis=0), "anis": nis.mean(axis=0), "rho": rho}
    print(f"{label:20s} mean ANEES {nees.mean():6.2f} (n=2)   "
          f"mean ANIS {nis.mean():5.2f} (m=1)   lag-1 rho {rho[0]:+.2f}")
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-kf-consistency
#| fig-cap: "Consistency diagnostics for the vessel filter over 50 Monte Carlo runs. Dashed lines are two-sided 95% chi-square bounds. The correct q sits inside the bounds with white innovations; too-small q is overconfident with strongly correlated innovations; too-large q is underconfident."
#| code-fold: true

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

k_axis = np.arange(1, n_steps + 1)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(3, 1, figsize=(8, 9))
for (label, res), color in zip(mc.items(), ["C0", "C3", "C2"]):
    axes[0].semilogy(k_axis, res["anees"], color=color, label=label)
    axes[1].semilogy(k_axis, res["anis"], color=color, label=label)
    axes[2].plot(np.arange(1, max_lag + 1), res["rho"], "o-", color=color, label=label)

for ax, dof, name in [(axes[0], 2, "ANEES"), (axes[1], 1, "ANIS")]:
    lo, hi = chi2_bounds(dof, n_runs)
    ax.axhline(lo, color="k", linestyle="--", linewidth=1)
    ax.axhline(hi, color="k", linestyle="--", linewidth=1)
    ax.set_ylabel(name)
    ax.set_xlabel("time step k")
    ax.grid(True, which="both", alpha=0.25)
axes[0].legend(loc="upper right")

bound = 1.96 / np.sqrt(n_steps)
axes[2].axhspan(-bound, bound, color="0.85", label="95% white-noise band")
axes[2].set_xlabel("lag j")
axes[2].set_ylabel(r"innovation autocorrelation $\hat\rho(j)$")
axes[2].set_ylim(-0.6, 0.9)
axes[2].grid(True, alpha=0.25)
axes[2].legend(loc="lower right", fontsize=8, ncol=2)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

Two lessons hide in those numbers. First, NEES is far more sensitive than NIS:
the too-small $q$ drives ANEES above 40 while ANIS only reaches about 2.5,
because the innovation covariance is dominated by the honest $\mathbf{R}$. A
filter can pass a casual NIS check while its state covariance is badly wrong, so
use NEES whenever you have any source of truth. Second, the whiteness panel
catches the too-small $q$ immediately from a single run, with no truth and no
Monte Carlo at all.

### A Practical Tuning Workflow {#sec-kf-tuning-workflow}

Tuning is not "increase random numbers until the plot looks better." A workable
sequence:

1. **Get $\mathbf{R}$ from the sensor.** Use the data sheet, then confirm with
   static data or a reference. $\mathbf{R}$ is usually the easier matrix to pin
   down, so pin it first and resist using it to fix process-model problems.
2. **Build $\mathbf{Q}$ from physics.** Use a continuous model, spectral
   densities, and @eq-kf-qd-integral or Van Loan, with IMU numbers from
   @sec-ins-errors-from-imu-specs where they apply.
3. **Check consistency in simulation with truth.** ANEES and ANIS inside their
   bounds when the simulator matches the filter model. If this fails, the bug is
   in the code.
4. **Check on real data with NIS and whiteness.** Look at the innovation mean
   (a nonzero mean is a bias or a frame error, not a tuning problem), the
   time-averaged NIS against its bounds, and the autocorrelation. Use the
   diagnostic table to decide whether $\mathbf{Q}$ or $\mathbf{R}$ is off.
5. **Adjust one thing at a time, then validate on data you did not tune on.**
   A filter tuned to one flight tends to be overfit to that flight.
6. **If no reasonable $\mathbf{Q}$ works, the model is wrong.** Persistent
   colored innovations usually mean a missing state such as a bias, a scale
   factor, or a lever arm. Add the state; do not inflate $\mathbf{Q}$ to hide it.

## Smoothing: The Rauch-Tung-Striebel Smoother {#sec-kf-smoothing}

A filter estimates $p(\mathbf{x}_k \mid \mathbf{z}_{1:k})$ because a vehicle has
to act now. But a surveyor processing a day of hydrographic data, an engineer
building a reference trajectory from flight-test data, or an investigator
reconstructing an accident is under no such constraint. They want
$p(\mathbf{x}_k \mid \mathbf{z}_{1:N})$, the estimate at each time using *all*
of the data, past and future. That is **smoothing**, and for linear Gaussian
systems the Rauch-Tung-Striebel (RTS) smoother computes it with one backward
pass over the stored filter output [@rauch1965].

The derivation is, once again, Gaussian conditioning. Given
$\mathbf{z}_{1:k}$, the states $\mathbf{x}_k$ and $\mathbf{x}_{k+1}$ are jointly
Gaussian with cross-covariance $\mathbf{P}_{k|k}\mathbf{F}_{k+1}^T$. Condition
$\mathbf{x}_k$ on $\mathbf{x}_{k+1}$ with @eq-kf-gaussian-conditioning:

$$
\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{x}_k \mid \mathbf{x}_{k+1}, \mathbf{z}_{1:k}]
=
\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{k|k} + \mathbf{J}_k(\mathbf{x}_{k+1} - \hat{\mathbf{x}}_{k+1|k}),
\qquad
\mathbf{J}_k = \mathbf{P}_{k|k}\mathbf{F}_{k+1}^T\mathbf{P}_{k+1|k}^{-1}.
$$

By the Markov property, once $\mathbf{x}_{k+1}$ is known the future
measurements $\mathbf{z}_{k+1:N}$ say nothing more about $\mathbf{x}_k$. So we
can average this conditional over the *smoothed* distribution of
$\mathbf{x}_{k+1}$, which we already have if we run backward from the end:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{k|N} &= \hat{\mathbf{x}}_{k|k} + \mathbf{J}_k\left(\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{k+1|N} - \hat{\mathbf{x}}_{k+1|k}\right), \\
\mathbf{P}_{k|N} &= \mathbf{P}_{k|k} + \mathbf{J}_k\left(\mathbf{P}_{k+1|N} - \mathbf{P}_{k+1|k}\right)\mathbf{J}_k^T.
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-kf-rts}

The recursion starts at $k = N$, where the filtered and smoothed estimates
coincide, and needs only the filter's stored priors and posteriors. This is why
`run_kf` saved `x_pred` and `P_pred`.

```{python}
#| label: kf-rts-smoother

import numpy as np


def rts_smoother(x_filt, P_filt, x_pred, P_pred, F):
    """Rauch-Tung-Striebel smoother for a time-invariant F.

    x_filt[k], P_filt[k] : posterior x_{k|k}, P_{k|k}
    x_pred[k], P_pred[k] : prior x_{k|k-1}, P_{k|k-1}
    """
    x_s, P_s = x_filt.copy(), P_filt.copy()
    for k in range(len(x_filt) - 2, -1, -1):
        # J = P_{k|k} F^T P_{k+1|k}^{-1}, computed with a solve.
        J = np.linalg.solve(P_pred[k + 1], F @ P_filt[k]).T
        x_s[k] = x_filt[k] + J @ (x_s[k + 1] - x_pred[k + 1])
        P_s[k] = P_filt[k] + J @ (P_s[k + 1] - P_pred[k + 1]) @ J.T
    return x_s, P_s


x_smooth, P_smooth = rts_smoother(kf["x"], kf["P"], kf["x_pred"], kf["P_pred"], F)
err_s = x_true - x_smooth
sigma_s = np.sqrt(np.stack([P_smooth[:, 0, 0], P_smooth[:, 1, 1]], axis=1))
for name, e in [("filter", err), ("smoother", err_s)]:
    print(f"{name:8s} RMSE: position {np.sqrt(np.mean(e[1:, 0]**2)):.2f} m, "
          f"speed {np.sqrt(np.mean(e[1:, 1]**2)):.2f} m/s")
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-kf-rts
#| fig-cap: "RTS smoothing of the vessel track. The smoother uses future measurements, so its errors and ±3σ bounds (dashed) are tighter than the filter's everywhere except the final step, where the two coincide."
#| code-fold: true

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(8, 6), sharex=True)
units = ["position error [m]", "speed error [m/s]"]
for i, ax in enumerate(axes):
    ax.plot(t, err[:, i], color="C0", alpha=0.6, label="filter error")
    ax.plot(t, 3 * sigma[:, i], ":", color="C0")
    ax.plot(t, -3 * sigma[:, i], ":", color="C0")
    ax.plot(t, err_s[:, i], color="C1", label="smoother error")
    ax.plot(t, 3 * sigma_s[:, i], "--", color="C1")
    ax.plot(t, -3 * sigma_s[:, i], "--", color="C1")
    ax.set_ylabel(units[i])
    ax.grid(True, alpha=0.25)
axes[0].set_ylim(-12, 12)
axes[1].set_ylim(-3, 3)
axes[0].legend(loc="upper right")
axes[1].set_xlabel("time [s]")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

The smoother is more than a post-processing trick. It is the exact solution of
a batch least-squares problem over the whole trajectory, with one cost term per
dynamics step and one per measurement, solved efficiently because each state
only talks to its neighbors in time. Draw that structure as a graph, with states
as nodes and cost terms as factors, and you have a **factor graph**. The
information-form view of @sec-information-filter and the SLAM back ends of
@sec-slam generalize exactly this idea to problems where the graph is not a
simple chain.

## Algorithm Summary {#sec-kf-algorithm-summary}

For each time step:

```text
predict:
    x_pred = F x + B u
    P_pred = F P F^T + Q            (or + L Q_u L^T for input noise)

update (when a measurement arrives):
    nu = z - H x_pred               innovation
    S  = H P_pred H^T + R           innovation covariance
    K  = P_pred H^T S^{-1}          via a linear solve
    x  = x_pred + K nu
    P  = (I - K H) P_pred (I - K H)^T + K R K^T     Joseph form
    log nu, S, and NIS = nu^T S^{-1} nu
```

The loop is short. The engineering is in $\mathbf{Q}$, $\mathbf{R}$, the choice
of state, and the discipline to check consistency before believing the output.

## Exercises {#sec-kf-exercises}

1. **Steady state by hand.** A hovering drone's barometric altitude is modeled
   as a random walk, $x_k = x_{k-1} + w_k$ with $\operatorname{Var}(w_k) = Q$,
   measured as $z_k = x_k + v_k$ with $\operatorname{Var}(v_k) = R$. Show that
   the steady-state prior variance $P_\text{ss}$ satisfies
   $P_\text{ss}^2 - QP_\text{ss} - QR = 0$, solve for $P_\text{ss}$ and the steady-state
   gain $K_\infty$, and evaluate both for $Q = 0.01\ \text{m}^2$ and
   $R = 0.25\ \text{m}^2$. Roughly how many past measurements does the
   steady-state filter effectively average?

2. **Why Joseph.** Starting from
   $\mathbf{e}_{k|k} = (\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{K}\mathbf{H})\mathbf{e}_{k|k-1} - \mathbf{K}\mathbf{v}_k$,
   derive @eq-kf-joseph. Show that it reduces to
   $(\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{K}\mathbf{H})\mathbf{P}_{k|k-1}$ when $\mathbf{K}$ is
   the optimal gain. Then, for a scalar problem with $P_{k|k-1} = 4$, $H = 1$,
   $R = 1$, and a deweighted gain $K = 0.4$, compute the posterior variance
   with both formulas. Which one is right, and is the wrong one optimistic or
   pessimistic?

3. **Constant-acceleration process noise.** For a three-state
   position-velocity-acceleration model driven by white jerk with spectral
   density $q$, derive $\mathbf{Q}_d$ from @eq-kf-qd-integral. Then verify your
   result numerically with `van_loan` for $\Delta t = 0.1$ s and $q = 2$.

4. **Diagnose the filter.** Extend the Monte Carlo cell to mis-specify
   $\mathbf{R}$ instead of $\mathbf{Q}$ (filter $\mathbf{R}$ ten times too small
   and ten times too large) and confirm the remaining rows of the diagnostic
   table in @sec-kf-reading-diagnostics. Report ANEES, ANIS, and the lag-one
   innovation correlation for all five cases.

5. **GNSS outage under a bridge.** In the vessel simulation, drop the GNSS fixes
   for $t \in [60, 90)$ s, as happens when a vessel passes under a wide bridge.
   Plot the position error with its $\pm 3\sigma$ bounds through the outage, and
   report the NIS of the first fix after reacquisition. Then run the RTS smoother
   on the same data and explain why the smoother's uncertainty peaks in the
   *middle* of the gap rather than at its end.

6. **What a Doppler log cannot see.** An underwater vehicle runs the
   constant-velocity model with only a speed measurement from a Doppler velocity
   log. Compute the observability matrix, identify the unobservable direction,
   and predict what $\mathbf{P}_{k|k}$ does for position over a long mission.
   Verify by modifying `run_kf`, then show that adding one position fix every
   60 s (for example from an acoustic USBL system) restores observability and
   bounds the position uncertainty.
